title: Equal Rights for Women (1969)
author: Shirley Chisholm
source: Address to the United States House of Representatives, May 21, 1969
citation: Chisholm, Shirley. 'Equal Rights for Women.' Congressional Record, 91st Congress, 1st Session, vol. 115, pt. 10, 21 May 1969, pp. 13693–13694.

sections.heading: Prejudice Against Women in America

epigraph.quote: Prejudice against women is still acceptable in our society. It is the unspoken assumption that women are second-class citizens.

paragraphs: Mr. Speaker, when a young woman graduates from college and starts looking for a job, she is likely to have a frustrating and disappointing experience. If she walks into an office for an interview, the first question she is asked is, 'Do you type?'

There is a calculated system of prejudice that lies just beneath the surface in the American economic and political structure. Why is it acceptable for women to be secretaries, librarians, and teachers, but not department heads, business executives, or senators? Why are women paid less than men for performing identical work?

As a Black person, I am no stranger to prejudice. But the truth is that in the political arena, I have met with far greater hostility, condescension, and resistance because of my sex than because of my race. Racism and sexism are twin evils, both rooted in the irrational need to preserve dominance and exclude talent.

sections.heading: The Moral and Legal Necessity of the Equal Rights Amendment

epigraph.quote: The Equal Rights Amendment is not a luxury or a special favor; it is a basic affirmation of constitutional justice.

paragraphs: Opponents of the Equal Rights Amendment claim that women are already protected by the Fourteenth Amendment. But courts have repeatedly held that women do not enjoy the same equal protection guarantees as racial minorities. Opponents argue that the ERA will destroy traditional families or subject women to harsh conditions.

These arguments are relics of a patriarchal mindset that views women as frail wards of the state rather than autonomous human beings. What we need in this country is an explicit constitutional guarantee that equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged on account of sex.

It is time to liberate the untapped potential of half of our population. By passing the Equal Rights Amendment, Congress will not only dismantle legal discrimination against women; it will reaffirm the foundational promise of American democracy.
